newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's BA/American decision seen before November.
newsitem.headline: EU's BA/American decision seen before November.

text.p: The European Commission expects to have ruled on the alliance between British Airways and AMR's American Airlines well before November.
Reacting to comments by BA's chairman Robert Ayling that the deal might be called off if it was not cleared by then, a Commission spokesman said: "We won't take that long".
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said last week that the Commission's probe into the alliance would certainly go beyond its August summer break.

EU competition officials are expected to meet their American counterparts this month, EU sources said, and the Commission may take a final stance on the alliance before Britain announces its decision.
Ayling said on Wednesday that BA wanted the deal approved by November when take-off and landing slots will be allocated for the summer 1998 season.

The alliance is being investigated by the Department of Transportation in the United States and by Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT). The Commission also started its own probe and must ensure any UK decision respects EU rules banning abuse of dominant position and agreements restrictive of competition in the Union.

The Commission has informed the British authorities of its view that the deal would dominate flights between the U.S. and London's congested Heathrow airport and that on 13 transatlantic routes it would eliminate competition altogether.

The EU sources appeared satisfied with a recent proposal by the U.S. General Accounting Office under which six U.S. airlines that do not currently serve Heathrow should obtain enough slots to operate 23 daily round-trip flights.
But they would not say whether the proposal reflected the Commission's own demands.

Any slots given to American airline rivals of BA and American were likely to benefit European companies as well because of the recent wave of transatlatic air alliances such as that between Lufthansa and United Airlines, on the one hand, and between Delta Air Lines, Swissair, Austrian Airlines and Sabena.
The OFT said in a preliminary ruling in December that it would clear the alliance provided the two airlines gave up 168 weekly take-off slots, enough for 12 daily round-trip flights.

The announcement triggered an angry warning from Van Miert who said in a letter to the then British Trade Secretary Ian Lang that this was not enough and that the EU would challenge such a decision in the European Court if necessary.
EU and British antitrust authorities now appear to be cooperating closely on the issue to avoid conflicting rulings.
